title: upgrade-preflight-and-runtime-failure-hunting-guide
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note is a pragmatic playbook for private deployments (VPC and on-prem) covering two related needs: preflight checks and Terraform module notes that reduce upgrade blast radius, and a compact troubleshooting/runbook for common install and runtime failures. Target audience: infra engineers, SREs, and on-call rotation engineers doing upgrades or responding to customer incidents.

High-level upgrade preflight checklist (ordered):
1) State and drift sanity
   - Ensure remote state is healthy and locked (S3+DynamoDB or GCS/locks). Command examples: terraform init, terraform plan -lock=true.
   - Run `terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan` and inspect diffs for unexpected resource replacements. If many replacements show up, do a targeted plan on changed modules.
   - Confirm no manual out-of-band changes in cluster: `kubectl get nodes,deploy,sts -A --show-labels` and compare to expected labels/taints.
2) Backups and rollback primitives
   - Snapshot critical etcd (on-prem k8s) or ensure cluster backup service completed within SLA window.
   - Export current Terraform state and store a copy with timestamp.
   - Ensure model artifacts + image registry tags are immutable (use digest pins) so rollback can redeploy previous artifacts.
3) Module/version pinning and provider compatibility
   - Pin module versions in root module (module "foo" { source = "./modules/foo" version = "v1.2.3" } or use git tag SHA). Avoid floating "latest".
   - Check provider version compatibility: run `terraform providers` and validate provider upgrade path in CHANGELOG.
4) Dry-run and canary path
   - Run upgrade in a staging environment with an identical module configuration but scaled down traffic.
   - If Dedicated/Private supports canaries, prepare routing policy to shift X% of traffic.
5) Capacity checks (nodes, GPU drivers, disk, network)
   - Verify GPU driver versions and Nvidia container toolkit on nodes that will run inference. `nvidia-smi` and `nvidia-container-cli --version` (or appropriate container runtime check).
   - Disk capacity: `df -h` on critical nodes and check kubelet eviction thresholds. Check overlayfs usage for containerd.
   - Check available ephemeral storage for model caching.
6) Secrets and KMS integration
   - Validate access to KMS/HSM from the private control plane: test decrypt/encrypt workflow on a test secret.
   - Validate cert rotation script runs and has required permissions.
7) Network and VPC endpoints
   - Confirm all required VPC endpoints (object storage, kms, ecr/registry) are reachable from private subnets. Use tcpdump/traceroute if necessary.
   - If using private container registries, test `docker pull` or `crane pull` from a node in the private network.

Terraform module notes and safe patterns (short):
- Use lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } only on resources that are irrecoverable (stateful DBs, HSM aliases). Document exceptions.
- Avoid embedding long shell scripts in module resources; move scripts to configmap-driven init containers so changes are visible at k8s level.
- Provide outputs for critical computed values (load balancer DNS, node pool autoscaler name) to simplify post-upgrade verification.
- Keep module inputs minimal and explicit: prefer booleans and maps to long concatenated strings.
- Gradual migration strategy: add new resources (blue) before removing old (green); use outputs to wire traffic switch.
- State move caution: when migrating state between backends, test on a copy and validate the resource addresses don't change unexpectedly.

Common upgrade gotchas (observed from field runs):
- Provider upgrade causes resource re-creation: typically due to provider-driven hashing of resources. Mitigation: read provider changelog and run targeted plans.
- Module refactor changed resource addresses (module.foo.aws_subnet.foo -> module.bar.aws_subnet.foo); leads to destroy/create. Use terraform state mv where needed.
- Image digest drift: pulling :latest causes nodes to have different images and invalid rollouts. Always use digest.

Compact smoke-test checklist (post-upgrade, quick to run, should be scripted in CI/CD):
1) Control plane health
   - k8s api: `kubectl get componentstatuses` and `kubectl get apiservices`
   - Check Redwood control-plane pods: `kubectl -n redwood-system get pods -o wide` (ready/available)
2) Model-serving readiness
   - Check model-serving deployment/statefulset: replicas ready matches desired. `kubectl -n redwood-serving get sts,deploy`
   - Small inference smoke: curl internal health endpoint: `curl -s -f http://redwood-serving.default.svc.cluster.local:8080/v1/health` expect 200 and json {"status":"ok"} (adjust for local API).
   - Run a lightweight generation request against a warm model: POST a 1-token prompt and assert response < 500ms (adjust SLO). If cold load expected, assert model load < configured threshold (e.g., 10s).
3) Router/load-balancer and TLS
   - Verify TLS certs presented by LB/ingress: `openssl s_client -connect lb.internal:443 -servername api.internal` check cert expiration and SAN.
4) Metrics and logs sanity
   - Check Prometheus targets: `up` metrics for essential exporters.
   - Confirm logs pipeline is ingesting (check last 5m logs for redwood-serving via loki/es).
5) Networking and egress policies
   - From a pod, test egress to object storage and KMS endpoints by running a short curl or aws s3 ls against a known bucket.
6) GPU quick smoke
   - Run a small CUDA job container that prints `nvidia-smi` and runs a tiny CUDA kernel. Validate container starts and GPU visible to container.
7) Token/costing telemetry
   - Generate a synthetic request and verify it appears in usage tables within 2–5 minutes.

Failure hunting guide (symptom -> quick triage -> deeper checks):
A) Symptom: model load failing with OOM or container crash
   Quick triage:
   - Inspect pod events: `kubectl describe pod <pod>` for OOMKilled or CrashLoopBackOff reasons.
   - Check node allocatable resources vs requested, and GPU count assigned.
   Deeper checks:
   - Review container logs for stack traces, and check model host memory maps.
   - Confirm quantized model size matches expected filesystem size and that image contains artifacts.
   - If using device plugin, verify plugin logs and Kubelet logs for GPU scheduling errors.

B) Symptom: high tail latency after upgrade
   Quick triage:
   - Check CPU steal, IO wait on nodes, and recent horizontal pod autoscaler events.
   - Look for new middleware introduced in upgrade (sidecars, additional proxy).
   Deeper checks:
   - Check batching config and server concurrency flags. An inadvertent change to batch sizes or queue timeouts can spike P95.
   - Inspect cache warming: if prefix/KV cache cleared on upgrade, first requests will be slow. Consider a warmup job to prepopulate caches.

C) Symptom: TLS handshake or mutual TLS failure with KMS/HSM
   Quick triage:
   - Validate cert chain and time sync on host (NTP).
   - Reproduce with openssl s_client to KMS endpoint.
   Deeper checks:
   - Validate cipher suites and TLS versions allowed; check HSM driver logs.
   - Check IAM/policy changes that might block access from private subnets.

D) Symptom: Terraform apply fails with checksum mismatch or resource in use
   Quick triage:
   - Re-run `terraform plan` and inspect which resource shows diff.
   - Check cloud provider console for resource locks or in-progress operations.
   Deeper checks:
   - If checksum mismatch on object storage, validate object registry content and rerun `terraform state rm` then import stable resource. Document steps for each provider to avoid state loss.

Useful commands and log filters (examples to copy into incident notes):
- `kubectl -n redwood-serving logs deploy/redwood-gateway --since=10m | sed -n '1,200p'`
- `kubectl -n redwood-serving get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -n 200`
- `journalctl -u containerd -n 500 --no-pager | grep -i nvidia`
- PromQL for sudden error spike: `sum(rate(http_server_errors_total{job="redwood-api"}[1m])) by (route)`
- Loki quick filter: `{app="redwood-serving"} |= "panic" or |= "OOMKilled"`

Runbook for escalations and postmortem anchors:
- If user-facing inference errors exceed threshold (configurable), escalate to on-call infra lead and notify solutions-engineering.
- Capture: timeline, terraform plan output, controller-manager/kubelet logs, node-level diagnostics, and any image digests involved.
- If rollback is chosen: pin previous module version, run `terraform apply -target=<resource>` only for resources that need revert, and run smoke-tests in reduced blast radius. Avoid full-destroy unless absolutely necessary.

Appendix: small Terraform debugging checklist (practical items)
- Export TF_LOG=DEBUG temporarily when reproducing a provider-level failure. Capture logs to secure storage.
- Use `terraform state show <resource>` to inspect live resource attributes; `terraform state mv` to fix address changes.
- When updating provider versions, read the provider migration guide and add migration notes to the module CHANGELOG.

Notes to self / TODOs for module owners:
- Add a documented warmup job that can be enabled during upgrades to pre-warm model caches.
- Add a terraform output with node pool autoscaler identifiers.
- Create a post-upgrade automation job that runs the compact smoke-test checklist and publishes a summary to the deployment channel.

End of document. If anything here is unclear, annotate inline and I will iterate.
